claim: The computational analysis of facial morphology using 3D imaging has been applied to fetal alcohol syndrome.
source: The computational analysis of facial morphology using 3D imaging has been applied to conditions such as fetal alcohol syndrome (Suttie et al., 2013), schizophrenia (Buckley et al., 2005; Hennessy et al., 2006, 2007) and autism (Aldridge et al., 2011).

evidence: Supported by citation to Aldridge et al., 2011

claim: 3D imaging studies have shown high discriminatory power in terms of classification but have relied on specialized imaging equipment and patient cooperation.
source: While 3D imaging studies have shown high discriminatory power in terms of classification they have relied on specialized imaging equipment and patient cooperation.

claim: Previous work with 2D images has relied on manual annotation of images, controlling lighting, pose and expression to allow consistent analyses.
source: Previous work with 2D images has relied on manual annotation of images, controlling lighting, pose and expression to allow consistent analyses.
evidence: Based on inference from previous literature discussion

claim: The database contains 2878 images, including 1515 healthy controls and 1363 pictures for eight known developmental disorders.
source: We first collected a database of 2878 images, including 1515 healthy controls and 1363 pictures for eight known developmental disorders from publically available sources across the internet (Table 1, references for image sources are available from Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Reported data from the study's database collection

claim: The computer vision algorithm detected and annotated 99.5% of tested faces correctly.
source: Across all images in our database, manual checking found that our algorithm detected and annotated 99.5% of tested faces correctly with accuracies in the range 6–60% of the width of an eye (individual feature point accuracies are provided in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The algorithm's annotation accuracies were in the range 6–60% of the width of an eye.
source: Across all images in our database, manual checking found that our algorithm detected and annotated 99.5% of tested faces correctly with accuracies in the range 6–60% of the width of an eye (individual feature point accuracies are provided in Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Classification analysis based on support vector machines provided similar accuracies to previous work, with an average classification accuracy of 94.4%.
source: We found that classification analysis based on support vector machines provided similar accuracies to previous work, despite disparities in image variability (average classification accuracy 94.4%, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and 'Materials and methods').

claim: The main sources of variation among images are lighting, pose, and facial expression, rather than phenotypic features.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of facial descriptor vectors illustrates that the main sources of variation among images are indeed lighting, pose, and facial expression, rather than phenotypic features (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: A kNN-classifier applied within Clinical Face Phenotype Space was able to correctly classify images with an accuracy of 99.5% using the leave-one-out method.
source: A kNN-classifier applied within Clinical Face Phenotype Space was able to correctly classify images with an accuracy of 99.5% using the leave-one-out method.

claim: The clustering of the eight syndromes within the database was improved by 11.0-fold on average.
source: On average, the clustering of the eight syndromes within the database was improved by 11.0-fold (geometric mean of improved clustering, CIF range 9.1–23.5, maximum possible mean 12.5; Figure 3).

claim: The CIF range for the eight syndromes was 9.1–23.5.
source: On average, the clustering of the eight syndromes within the database was improved by 11.0-fold (geometric mean of improved clustering, CIF range 9.1–23.5, maximum possible mean 12.5; Figure 3).

claim: The search space reduction for syndromes not used in training was on average 27.6-fold better than random chance.
source: The search space reduction was on average 27.6-fold better than random chance (CIF range 1.0–700.0, maximum possible average CIF was 150.0; Figure 4A).
evidence: Reported data from clustering analysis of additional syndromes

claim: The CIF range for syndromes not used in training was 1.0–700.0.
source: The search space reduction was on average 27.6-fold better than random chance (CIF range 1.0–700.0, maximum possible average CIF was 150.0; Figure 4A).
evidence: Reported data from clustering analysis of additional syndromes

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space makes it 27.6-fold easier to make the correct diagnosis among 2754 patients' faces associated with any of 90 syndromes.
source: That is to say, that among 2754 patients' faces associated with any of 90 syndromes Clinical Face Phenotype Space makes it 27.6-fold easier to make the correct diagnosis.

claim: For the eight initial syndromes used to construct Clinical Face Phenotype Space, 93.1% are correctly classified as the top rank.
source: We find that for the eight initial syndromes used to construct Clinical Face Phenotype Space, 93.1% (range 81.0–99.2%) are correctly classified as the top rank, cumulatively converging on 99.1% (95.8–100%) by the 20th rank (Figure 4B).

claim: For the eight initial syndromes, classification accuracy cumulatively converges on 99.1% by the 20th rank.
source: We find that for the eight initial syndromes used to construct Clinical Face Phenotype Space, 93.1% (range 81.0–99.2%) are correctly classified as the top rank, cumulatively converging on 99.1% (95.8–100%) by the 20th rank (Figure 4B).

claim: For syndromes not part of the Clinical Face Phenotype Space training, the classification accuracies positively correlated strongly with the number of instances in the database.
source: Of syndromes not part of the Clinical Face Phenotype Space training, the classification accuracies positively correlated strongly with the number of instances in the database (Figure 4B).

claim: For the 20 syndromes where the database held 5 or fewer examples, the algorithm classifies on average 20.3% correctly by the 6th rank.
source: For the 20 syndromes where the database held 5 or fewer examples (Table 1), we classify on average 20.3% correctly by the 6th rank (exceeding 16.3-fold better than by chance alone).

claim: For syndromes with 5 or fewer examples, classification performance exceeds 16.3-fold better than by chance alone.
source: For the 20 syndromes where the database held 5 or fewer examples (Table 1), we classify on average 20.3% correctly by the 6th rank (exceeding 16.3-fold better than by chance alone).

claim: The 2 PACS1 cases placed within Clinical Face Phenotype Space have a p0p1 value of 1.05.
source: The 2 PACS1 cases reported by Schuurs-Hoeijmakers et al. (2012) placed within Clinical Face Phenotype Space have a p0p1 value of 1.05 meaning that they are 5% closer to one another than the geometric mean of the distances to their 20 nearest neighbors.

claim: The 2 PACS1 cases are 5% closer to one another than the geometric mean of the distances to their 20 nearest neighbors.
source: The 2 PACS1 cases reported by Schuurs-Hoeijmakers et al. (2012) placed within Clinical Face Phenotype Space have a p0p1 value of 1.05 meaning that they are 5% closer to one another than the geometric mean of the distances to their 20 nearest neighbors.

claim: The search space to find the 2 PACS1 cases has been reduced approximately 690.4-fold.
source: Taking into account that this is a local density estimate among 2754 faces in Clinical Face Phenotype Space, the search space to find them has been reduced ∼690.4-fold (CIF, see 'Materials and methods').

claim: The distance in Clinical Face Phenotype Space is significantly shorter between syndromes associated to genes with protein interaction distances of 1, 2, or 3 compared with syndromes with 4 or no known interactions.
source: The distance in Clinical Face Phenotype Space is significantly shorter between syndromes associated to genes with protein interaction distances of 1, 2, or 3 compared with syndromes with 4 or no known interactions (p< 0.01, p< 0.05 and p< 0.001 respectively, Figure 5).
evidence: Reported data from protein-protein interaction analysis with statistical testing

claim: The distance in Clinical Face Phenotype Space partly recapitulates the functional relatedness of underlying developmental processes known to be disrupted in genetic diseases.
source: This demonstrates that the distance in Clinical Face Phenotype Space partly recapitulates the functional relatedness of underlying developmental processes known to be disrupted in genetic diseases.
evidence: Inferred from the protein-protein interaction distance analysis

claim: The approach extracts phenotypic information from ordinary non-clinical photographs.
source: This algorithm extracts phenotypic information from ordinary non-clinical photographs and, using machine learning, models human facial dysmorphisms in a multidimensional 'Clinical Face Phenotype Space'.

claim: The approach narrows the search space of potential diagnoses for patients with suspected developmental disorders by 27.6-fold.
source: Consequently, the approach will aid clinicians by greatly narrowing (by 27.6-fold) the search space of potential diagnoses for patients with suspected developmental disorders.

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space allows the clustering of patients by phenotype even when no known syndrome diagnosis exists.
source: Furthermore, this Clinical Face Phenotype Space allows the clustering of patients by phenotype even when no known syndrome diagnosis exists, thereby aiding disease identification.

claim: The approach provides a novel method for inferring causative genetic variants from clinical sequencing data through functional genetic pathway comparisons.
source: We demonstrate that this approach provides a novel method for inferring causative genetic variants from clinical sequencing data through functional genetic pathway comparisons.

source: Manual annotation of facial features points was performed on all images to allow training and testing of an automated annotation algorithm.

claim: The approach is fully automated.

claim: The approach provides objective and consistent computational descriptions of facial gestalt.
source: The approach is fully automated and provides objective and consistent computational descriptions of facial gestalt.

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space is robust to spurious variations such as lighting, pose, and image quality.
source: We have ensured that Clinical Face Phenotype Space is robust to spurious variations such as lighting, pose, and image quality which would otherwise bias analyses.

claim: The approach will increase the power of inferring causative variants in previously unidentified genetic disease.
source: Our method both greatly narrows the search space for investigating known disorders and will increase the power of inferring causative variants in previously unidentified genetic disease.

claim: 3100 images were collected and manually annotated for training of the algorithms.
source: 3100 images were collected and manually annotated for training of the algorithms.

claim: 2878 images were successfully annotated by the automatic pipeline.
source: Of these 2878 were successfully annotated by the automatic pipeline and are reported in the database counts of Table 1.

claim: The algorithm takes advantage of a variety of facial detection algorithms including OpenCV, Viola Jones, and Everingham.
source: Our approach takes advantage of a variety of facial detection algorithms (OpenCV [Bradski, 2000], Viola Jones [Viola and Jones, 2001] and Everingham [Everingham et al., 2009]) and custom learning (consensus of exemplars [Belhumeur et al., 2011]) to accurately place feature points on a given face ('Materials and methods').

claim: The algorithm uses consensus of exemplars for custom learning.
source: Our approach takes advantage of a variety of facial detection algorithms (OpenCV [Bradski, 2000], Viola Jones [Viola and Jones, 2001] and Everingham [Everingham et al., 2009]) and custom learning (consensus of exemplars [Belhumeur et al., 2011]) to accurately place feature points on a given face ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Description of the algorithm's components with citation to Belhumeur et al., 2011

claim: An Active Appearance Model was used to calculate an average face within any set of images.
source: We used an Active Appearance Model ('Materials and methods') to calculate an average face within any set of images, representing consistent shape and appearance features within the group (Figure 1B and animated morphs in Figure 2).

claim: The average faces for each syndrome show that the algorithm effectively captures characteristic features of dysmorphic syndromes.
source: The average faces for each syndrome show that the algorithm effectively captures characteristic features of dysmorphic syndromes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The algorithm extracts a feature vector describing appearance of the surrounding patch for each feature point.
source: For each feature point, the algorithm extracts a feature vector describing appearance of the surrounding patch.

claim: The algorithm constructs a feature vector describing shape based on the relative pairwise distances between all feature points.
source: The algorithm then constructs a feature vector describing shape based on the relative pairwise distances between all feature points ('Materials and methods').

claim: Metric Learning using a Large Margin Nearest Neighbor approach was performed for the eight syndromes in the database.
source: We next performed Metric Learning using a Large Margin Nearest Neighbor (Weinberger and Saul, 2009) approach for the eight syndromes in the database.
evidence: Description of the method used with citation

claim: Large Margin Nearest Neighbor linearly transformed the multidimensional space of PCA feature vectors to optimize the separation of syndromes.
source: This approach linearly transformed the multidimensional space of PCA feature vectors to optimize the separation of syndromes: dimensions informative for dysmorphism phenotypes are expanded while uninformative dimensions are compressed (thus changing the relative importance for clustering).

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space is a 270 dimensional space.
source: We denote the resulting transformed 270 dimensional space as 'Clinical Face Phenotype Space' (see 'Materials and methods').

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space clusters patient faces based on diagnostically relevant phenotypic features, while tolerating spurious variation.
source: Due to its design, Clinical Face Phenotype Space clusters patient faces based on diagnostically relevant phenotypic features, while tolerating spurious variation.

claim: In Clinical Face Phenotype Space, feature dimensions that reflected known spurious variation such as lighting and head orientation were compressed.
source: For these faces feature dimensions that reflected known spurious variation such as lighting and head orientation were compressed and hence were of less relevance for clustering (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Images were analyzed irrespective of the subject's age, gender, facial expression or ethnicity or the background scenery.
source: Photos were analyzed irrespective of the subject's age, gender, facial expression or ethnicity or the background scenery.

claim: The database includes 75 syndromes from the Gorlin collection.
source: We had access to 75 syndromes from the Gorlin collection (a kind gift curated and annotated by Professor Raoul Hennekam, Academic Medical Center, University of Amsterdam), which we supplemented with additional images of 22q11, Marfan and Sotos syndromes.

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space is an effective approach to the identification of multiple individuals sharing ultra-rare, previously undocumented, genetic disorders.
source: This demonstrates that Clinical Face Phenotype Space is an effective approach to the identification of multiple individuals sharing ultra-rare, previously undocumented, genetic disorders.

claim: Protein–protein interaction distances of 1–3 for genetically characterized syndromes are associated with significantly shorter Euclidean distance between syndromes in Clinical Face Phenotype Space.
source: Protein–protein interaction distances of 1–3 for genetically characterized syndromes are associated with significantly shorter Euclidean distance (arbitrary units) between syndromes in Clinical Face Phenotype Space as compared to syndromes with distance 4 or no known interaction distance (shown in orange) (Kruskal–Wallis tests with Bonferroni corrected p-values indicated as *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001).
evidence: Reported data from protein-protein interaction analysis shown in Figure 5

claim: The Spearman correlation across all protein-protein interaction distances was r = 0.09, p<0.001.
source: The Spearman correlation across all distances was r = 0.09, p<0.001.

claim: For any given image located in Clinical Face Phenotype Space, confidence ranked classifications to known disorders can be obtained.
source: For any given image located in Clinical Face Phenotype Space, we obtain confidence ranked classifications to known disorders (see 'Materials and methods' and Figure 4—figure supplement 4).

claim: A probabilistic ranking of similar syndromes is obtained through nearest neighbor representation compared to random expectation of clustering among the 90 syndromes and 2754 faces.
source: For any given query image, a probabilistic ranking of similar syndromes is obtained through nearest neighbor representation compared to random expectation of clustering among the 90 syndromes and 2754 faces.

claim: The classification confidence for a particular disorder depends on its location within the space and on the local densities of similar faces.
source: The classification confidence for a particular disorder depends on its location within the space, but also on the local densities of similar faces.

claim: A p0p1 value exceeding 1 indicates a potentially new cluster.
source: The metric estimates the relative closeness of two faces given an average local density with the space: a p0p1 value exceeding 1 indicates a potentially new cluster, see 'Materials and methods'.

claim: The combination of syndrome clustering and de novo similarity metrics should aid the diagnosis of known syndromes.
source: The combination of syndrome clustering and de novo similarity metrics should aid the diagnosis of known syndromes and provides a means of clustering patients where no documented diagnosis exists.

source: The combination of syndrome clustering and de novo similarity metrics should aid the diagnosis of known syndromes and provides a means of clustering patients where no documented diagnosis exists.

claim: The approach is able to describe and discriminate between syndromes with a comparable accuracy to previous studies.

(2) The spectrum of phenotypes represented was limited. (3) The average image quality in the database was low.

source: As Clinical Face Phenotype Space is developed and populated with more individuals, the predictive power to infer novel causative genetics would be expected to increase linearly until it asymptotically approaches a theoretical maximum.

claim: There are three anticipated primary applications for Clinical Face Phenotype Space in a clinical setting: narrowing the search space for documented developmental disorders, identifying multiple people that share an ultra-rare genetic disorders and aiding the inference of causative variants in clinical genetic sequencing.
source: There are three anticipated primary applications for Clinical Face Phenotype Space in a clinical setting: narrowing the search space for documented developmental disorders, identifying multiple people that share an ultra-rare genetic disorders and aiding the inference of causative variants in clinical genetic sequencing (Figure 4).

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space is envisaged to become a standard tool to support clinical genetic counseling.
source: We envisage Clinical Face Phenotype Space becoming a standard tool to support clinical genetic counseling.

claim: The approach is available to any clinician worldwide with access to a camera and a computer.
source: Since any normal 2D image can be analyzed, this approach is available to any clinician worldwide with access to a camera and a computer.

claim: A photograph will enable automatic digital phenotyping, and its placement in Clinical Face Phenotype Space will provide an unbiased list of candidate clinical hypotheses.
source: A photograph will enable automatic digital phenotyping, and its placement in Clinical Face Phenotype Space will provide an unbiased list of candidate clinical hypotheses (exemplified in Figure 6).
evidence: Description of the approach's capabilities with example

claim: Future developments of Clinical Face Phenotype Space will also identify sub-phenotypes or comorbidities.
source: We anticipate that future developments of Clinical Face Phenotype Space will also identify sub-phenotypes or comorbidities.

claim: Where no known genetic disease or variant can be assigned, Clinical Face Phenotype Space can identify other patients with phenotypic similarities empowering the identification of ultra-rare genetic disorders.
source: Where no known genetic disease or variant can be assigned, Clinical Face Phenotype Space can identify other patients with phenotypic similarities empowering the identification of ultra-rare genetic disorders.

claim: Abraham Lincoln is thought to have had a marfanoid disorder, if not Marfan syndrome.
source: Abraham Lincoln. The former US President is thought to have had a marfanoid disorder, if not Marfan syndrome (Gordon, 1962; Sotos, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordon, 1962; Sotos, 2012

claim: The classification of Marfan for Abraham Lincoln was not successfully assigned in the first instance as there were only 18 faces of individuals with Marfan in the database.
source: As expected, the classification of Marfan is not successfully assigned in the first instance as there were only 18 faces of individuals with Marfan in the database (making this an example of a difficult case with the current database).
evidence: Reported data from classification example shown in Figure 6B

claim: Marfan was the seventh suggestion for Abraham Lincoln's classification, despite this being among 90 different syndromes and 2754 faces.
source: However, the seventh suggestion is Marfan, despite this being among 90 different syndromes and 2754 faces.
evidence: Reported data from classification example shown in Figure 6B

claim: The conjunction of a computer vision and machine learning algorithm with Clinical Face Phenotype Space makes this approach high-throughput, automatic, objective, and broadly accessible with existing digital photography and computers.
source: The conjunction of a computer vision and machine learning algorithm with Clinical Face Phenotype Space makes this approach high-throughput, automatic, objective, and broadly accessible with existing digital photography and computers.

claim: Computer vision for aiding diagnosis of developmental disorders in clinical genetics will be tenable and broadly applicable in the near future.
source: Computer vision for aiding diagnosis of developmental disorders in clinical genetics will be tenable and broadly applicable in the near future.

claim: Images were collected through publically available resources online accessible though search terms relating to each syndrome, primarily through support group pages and awareness event photographs.
source: Images were collected through publically available resources online accessible though search terms relating to each syndrome, primarily through support group pages and awareness event photographs.

claim: The following two exclusion criteria were applied to the images: 1. The face needed to be clearly visible and oriented so that both eyes were visible. 2. The correct diagnosis was confirmed by an expert clinician (DRF).
source: The following two exclusion criteria were applied to the images: 1. The face needed to be clearly visible and oriented so that both eyes were visible. 2. The correct diagnosis was confirmed by an expert clinician (DRF).

claim: Variation in lighting, image resolution, pose, and occlusions has only been restricted when it obscures the facial characteristics.
source: Variation in lighting, image resolution, pose, and occlusions has only been restricted when it obscures the facial characteristics (such as a hand covering the face).

claim: The authors sought to avoid multiple images of the same individual at the same age in the database.
source: We also sought to avoid multiple images of the same individual at the same age in the database.

claim: No further restrictions were placed on variations in pose, facial expression, lighting, occlusions, or image quality.
source: No further restrictions were placed on variations in pose, facial expression, lighting, occlusions, or image quality.

claim: The manner and method by which images were collected from publically available sources and stored were acceptable research practices and do not require special consent from a Research Ethics Committee.
source: The manner and method by which images were collected from publically available sources and stored were acceptable research practices and do not require special consent from a Research Ethics Committee.

claim: Advice from legal services, research ethics board members and the Information Commissioner's Office (UK) was sought in arriving at the conclusion that no special consent was required.
source: Advice from legal services, research ethics board members and the Information Commissioner's Office (UK) was sought in arriving at this conclusion.

claim: MATLAB with OpenCV was used to write scripts and functions for the algorithm.
source: MATLAB (MATLAB. R2011b Natick, Massachusetts: the MathWorks Inc.) with OpenCV (Bradski, 2000) was used to write scripts and functions for the algorithm.

claim: To identify a putative face in the photo, previously published algorithms were used.
source: To identify a putative face in the photo, we used previously published algorithms (Viola and Jones, 2001).

claim: Within a box bounding the face, a pictorial structure model was used to identify 9 central facial feature points.
source: Within a box bounding the face, a pictorial structure model was used to identify 9 central facial feature points (Everingham et al., 2009), which then were used to initialize the placement of an additional 27 feature points.

claim: The 9 central facial feature points were used to initialize the placement of an additional 27 feature points.
source: Within a box bounding the face, a pictorial structure model was used to identify 9 central facial feature points (Everingham et al., 2009), which then were used to initialize the placement of an additional 27 feature points.

claim: The resulting facial mesh structure was fitted to the image using Active Appearance Models to generate average face visualizations.
source: The resulting facial mesh structure was fitted to the image using Active Appearance Models (AAMs) (Cootes et al., 1998) to generate average face visualizations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: The placement of the 36 feature points was refined using custom written scripts based on consensus of exemplars.
source: The placement of the 36 feature points was also further refined using custom written scripts based on consensus of exemplars (Belhumeur et al., 2011) (see Methods).

claim: The appearance feature vector is a concatenation of the pixel intensities of patches around the 9 inner facial feature points.
source: From the fitted constellation of facial landmarks two feature vectors were extracted. (1) The appearance as a concatenation of the pixel intensities of patches around the 9 inner facial feature points.

claim: The shape vector was constructed as the normalized pairwise distances between all 36 facial feature points.
source: (2) The shape vector was constructed as the normalized pairwise distances between all 36 facial feature points.

claim: Face detection was achieved using the OpenCV implementation of the Viola–Jones object detection framework.
source: Face detection was achieved using the OpenCV (Bradski, 2000) implementation of the Viola–Jones object detection framework (using Haar like features and a cascade of classifiers) (Viola and Jones, 2001).

claim: The output of face detection takes the form of a square bounding box delimiting the area of the picture where the face was found.
source: The output takes the form of a square bounding box delimiting the area of the picture where the face was found.

claim: Manual annotation of the 36 feature points was performed on 3100 of the images in the image collection.
source: Manual annotation of the 36 feature points was performed on 3100 of the images in the image collection.

claim: Manual annotations were used as the ground truth reference point for all subsequent training and test sets for evaluations of automated facial landmark annotation accuracies.
source: These were used as the ground truth reference point for all subsequent training and test sets for evaluations of automated facial landmark annotation accuracies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The 9 landmarks annotated by the FLA module were the medial and lateral canthi of the eyes, each subnasale, columella and the left and right vermilion border lateral midpoints.
source: The 9 landmarks in that set were the medial and lateral canthi of the eyes, each subnasale, columella and the left and right vermilion border lateral midpoints.

claim: The FLA used the returned bounding box to approximate the location and size of the face to be annotated.
source: The FLA used the returned bounding box to approximate the location and size of the face to be annotated.

claim: Automatic annotation relies on a generative model of feature point position combined with a discriminative model of appearances.
source: Automatic annotation relies on a generative model of feature point position combined with a discriminative model of appearances.

claim: The joint model was based on the parts-based pictorial structure representation introduced by Fischler and Elschlager (1973).
source: This joint model was based on the parts-based pictorial structure representation introduced by Fischler and Elschlager (1973).
evidence: Description of the model with citation

claim: For a given bounding box, the FLA module returns both a constellation of 9 landmarks and a corresponding confidence index computed via appearance mismatch with the model.
source: For a given bounding box, the FLA module returns both a constellation of 9 landmarks and a corresponding confidence index computed via appearance mismatch with the model.

claim: The images were transformed iteratively by mirror imaging, partial rotations (±45°), and by adding a frame around the image to produce 100 transformations of the original.
source: The images were transformed iteratively by mirror imaging, partial rotations (±45°), and by adding a frame around the image to produce 100 transformations of the original.
evidence: Description of the improved annotation method

claim: A consensus map is constructed by confidence weighted averaging of high confidence feature annotations thus reducing the number of spurious annotations and increasing annotation accuracy.
source: A consensus map is constructed by confidence weighted averaging of high confidence feature annotations thus reducing the number of spurious annotations and increasing annotation accuracy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of the improved annotation method

claim: Consensus of exemplar relies on part base classifiers used to localize potential candidate points and a database of face exemplars used to introduce a shape prior in the search for the best constellation.
source: Consensus of exemplar (CoE) relies on part base classifiers used to localize potential candidate points and a database of face exemplars used to introduce a shape prior in the search for the best constellation.

claim: 1000 exemplar faces are sampled from among the controls in the database.
source: For each of the facial feature points in C36, we delimited a region of interest (ROI) for the algorithm to consider using the following heuristic: 1000 exemplar faces are sample from among the controls in the database (Table 1).

claim: For each exemplar face, the C9 was registered to the C9 of the query face using Procrustes algorithm.
source: For each exemplar face i, we registered the C9i to the C9 of our query face using Procrustes algorithm.

claim: The top 20 exemplars were used to map their C36 to the query face using the transform obtained during registration.
source: The top 20 exemplars were used to map their C36i to the query face using the transform Ti obtained during registration.

claim: A consensus C36 for the query face was derived by averaging all registered C36.
source: A consensus C36 for the query face was then derived by averaging all registered C36i.

claim: For each feature point in C36, a square ROI centered on the consensus point with two palpebral fissures length dimensions was defined.
source: Finally, for each feature point in C36, we defined a square ROI centered on the consensus point with two palpebral fissures (PF) length dimensions.

claim: Support Vector Machine classifiers using Gaussian kernels were trained to recognize each feature point in C36.
source: Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifiers (using Gaussian kernels) were trained to recognize each feature point in C36.

claim: A database of manually annotated control patients was used to obtain positive and negative training sets for each part classifier.
source: We used a database of manually annotated control patients to obtain positive and negative training sets for each part classifier.

claim: The feature vector associated with a particular feature point was obtained by cropping a square patch centered on this point and describing its pixel content with a pyramidal histogram of gradients.
source: The feature vector associated with a particular feature point was obtained by cropping a square patch centered on this point and describing its pixel content with a pyramidal histogram of gradients (PHOG).

claim: Each of the 36 ROIs was submitted to the corresponding part detector to obtain a set of 20 potential candidates for each part within the ROI.
source: Going back to the query face, each of the 36 ROIs was submitted to the corresponding part detector. From this we obtained a set of 20 potential candidates (PC) for each part within the ROI (where candidates were sorted based on the classifier decision values).

claim: Exemplars of C36 were randomly sampled from the control database and registered to the query face in order to enforce a shape prior.
source: Next, we randomly sampled exemplars of C36 from the control database and registered them to the query face in order to enforce a shape prior.

claim: The top 20 registered C36 were retained based on scoring by submitting feature points to the part classifiers.
source: The registered C36i were scored by submitting its feature points to the part classifiers. We retained the top 20 C36i.

claim: Each feature point of the final C36 for the query was derived independently as a consensus between probability density maps based on the PCs and the classifier decision values over the corresponding ROI.
source: Finally, each feature point of the final C36 for the query was derived independently as a consensus between probability density maps based on the PCs and the classifier decision values over the corresponding ROI.

claim: Four additional points were generated from the set of 9 inner points: left and right center of the eye, nasion, and center of the mouth.
source: Using the set of 9 inner points annotated to the face by the FLA module and refined by the CoE module, four additional points were generated: left and right center of the eye, nasion (between the eyes) and center of the mouth.

claim: The points were used to register the face via an affine transformation to a canonical set of corresponding points.
source: The points were then used to register the face, via an affine transformation T, to a canonical set of corresponding points (face shape template).

claim: Circular patches were generated around the canonical points which were mapped back to the original picture using the inverse of the transformation.
source: Next, circular patches were generated around the canonical points which were mapped back to the original picture using the inverse of T.

claim: The appearance feature vector was obtained by a concatenation of the pixel gray-scale content of the 13 cropped patches with a size of 1937.
source: The appearance feature vector was obtained by a concatenation of the pixel gray-scale content of the 13 cropped patches (size of the feature vector = 1937).

claim: The gain in terms of discriminative power and relevant feature extracted was negligible compared to the computational cost in terms of memory consumption for further processing of patch content.
source: While patch content could be further processed before concatenation (gradients, HOG, PHOG, SIFT, Gabor Filter, Local binary Pattern, etc) the gain in terms of discriminative power and relevant feature extracted was negligible compared to the computational cost in terms of memory consumption.
evidence: Justification for method choice based on testing

claim: The shape features vector was built from the constellation of the 36 landmarks annotations from the CoE module as a vector of pair-wise distances through the constellation, resulting in a feature vector with 630 elements.
source: The features vector was built from the constellation of the 36 landmarks annotations from the CoE module. We described the face shape as a vector d, the set of pair-wise distances through the constellation, resulting in a feature vector with 630 elements.

claim: To compare different constellations, each was registered via Procrustes transformation to the average constellation of the AAM model.
source: To compare the different constellations, each was registered via Procrustes transformation to the average constellation of the AAM model (canonical face mesh, see below).

claim: The vector of pair-wise distances was normalized so that any distance variations were relative to the corresponding distances measured on the average control face template.
source: The vector of pair-wise distances was then normalized so that any distance variations were relative to the corresponding distances measured on the average control face template.

claim: A training set was constructed by manual annotation of 3100 patient images with the 36 landmarks.
source: We constructed a training set by manual annotation of 3100 patient images with the 36 landmarks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: All constellations were registered together using an iterative Procrustes algorithm.
source: All constellations were registered together using an iterative Procrustes algorithm.

claim: The average constellation was computed and used as a reference with which to build a canonical face mesh via Delaunay triangulation.
source: We computed the average constellation and used it as a reference with which to build a canonical face mesh via Delaunay triangulation.
evidence: Description of the mesh construction method

claim: Based on the obtained triangulation, a face mesh was generated dividing each patient's face into sub-regions.
source: Based on the obtained triangulation, we generated a face mesh dividing each patient's face into sub-regions.
evidence: Description of the mesh generation method

claim: Using piecewise affine warping, the pixel content of each sub-region was independently mapped to the corresponding triangle in the canonical face mesh.
source: Using piecewise affine warping, we independently mapped the pixel content of each sub-region to the corresponding triangle in the canonical face mesh.

claim: A registered version of each patient's facial appearance was obtained through the warping process.
source: We thus obtained a registered version of each patient's facial appearance.
evidence: Description of the output of the warping process

claim: Shapes and appearance registrations were used in a principal component analysis to generate both the shape and appearance models for use with the AAM.
source: Shapes and appearance registrations were used in a principal component analysis (PCA) to generate both the shape and appearance models for use with the AAM.
evidence: Description of the model generation method

claim: Average faces were created from the images of patient with the same genetic disorder using AAM statistical models.
source: Using the AAM statistical models of shape and appearance that derive from the training of the AAM, we created a visual representation of canonical traits/phenotypes. Average faces were created from the images of patient with the same genetic disorder.

claim: AAM models were generated for each group, and after registration of the constellations to each, the average shape constellation was derived.
source: AAM models were generated for each group, and after registration of the constellations (annotation) to each we derived the average shape constellation.

claim: A face mesh was generated from the average shape constellations by triangulation.
source: A face mesh was generated from these constellations by triangulation (Delaunay) and the appearance of each individual was mapped to the average face mesh by piecewise affine warping.

claim: The average face mesh recapitulated the canonical phenotype of the syndromes.
source: Thus, this average face mesh recapitulated the canonical phenotype of the syndromes.
evidence: Description of the average face mesh properties

claim: Morphs between control and syndrome faces were created by registering appearance to the average shape of the controls.
source: Furthermore, we created morphs between control and syndrome faces by registering appearance to the average shape of the controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Libsvm was employed to perform classification.
source: We employed Libsvm to perform classification.

claim: The accuracies based on the raw feature vectors were comparable to accuracies reported in previous studies.
source: The accuracies based on the raw feature vectors were comparable to accuracies reported in previous studies (Boehringer et al., 2006, 2011).
evidence: Comparison with previous work supported by citations

claim: SVM classifiers were trained on both shape and appearance feature vectors separately for each 36 pairwise combination of control and 8 syndromes.
source: SVM classifiers were trained on both shape and appearance feature vectors separately for each 36 pairwise combination of control and 8 syndromes (Table 1).

claim: Each binary classification was repeated 10 times with randomly generated positive/negative training and test sets with a 4:1 ratio.
source: Each binary classification was repeated 10 times with randomly generated positive/negative training and test sets with a 4:1 ratio.

claim: A total accuracy when fusing information from shape and appearance feature vectors based SVMs was estimated by summing decision values returned by the shape and appearance classifiers respectively.
source: We estimate a total accuracy when fusing information from shape and appearance feature vectors based SVMs by summing decision values returned by the shape and appearance classifiers respectively.

claim: In all classification experiments, both original and mirror versions of each image were used.
source: In all classification experiments, we used both original and mirror versions of each image.

claim: Decision values were tuned to give equal error rates (the number of false positives = number of false negatives).
source: Decision values were tuned to give equal error rates (the number of false positives = number of false negatives).

claim: For each instance in the test set, two decision values were obtained from submitting the original and mirror versions separately to the classifier.
source: With the trained SVM models, we next submitted the sets G1te + G2te and G1tem + G2tem separately to the classifier. Thus, for each instance in the test set we obtained two decision values.

claim: The final classification was determined by the sum of the decision values from original and mirror versions.
source: The final classification was determined by the sum of the decision values.

claim: Each of the 8 syndrome groups was randomly split into training and test sets with a ratio of 4:1 for forced choice classification.
source: Each of the 8 syndrome groups was randomly split into training and test sets with a ratio of 4:1.
evidence: Description of forced choice classification experiments

claim: The training sets were used to train a linear binary SVM classifier for each of the 28 pairs in forced choice classification.
source: We used the training sets to train a linear binary SVM classifier for each of the 28 pairs.
evidence: Description of forced choice classification experiments

claim: Each image in the training set was submitted to all 28 classifiers in forced choice classification.
source: Each image in the training set was submitted to all 28 classifiers.
evidence: Description of forced choice classification experiments

claim: The decision value returned by each classifier was used as a probabilistic estimate for the test instance to belong to the positive class.
source: The decision value was returned by each classified and used as a probabilistic estimate P for the test instance to belong to the positive class.
evidence: Description of forced choice classification method

claim: After presenting instance i to the binary classifier distinguishing syndrome j from syndrome k, instance i was assigned a vote of weight P for syndrome j and a vote of weight 1-P for syndrome k.
source: Thus, after presenting instance i to the binary classifier distinguishing syndrome j (positive) from syndrome k (negative), we assigned i a vote of weight P for syndrome j and a vote of weight 1-P for syndrome k.
evidence: Description of forced choice classification method

claim: After summation of the votes from the 28 classifiers, the instance was labeled as belonging to the syndrome diagnosis with the highest probability.
source: After summation of the votes from the 28 classifiers, the instance i was labeled as belonging to the syndrome diagnosis with the highest probability.
evidence: Description of forced choice classification method

claim: PCA was performed on the shape and appearance feature vectors to reduce dimensionality from 2567 to a concatenation of 340 orthogonal vectors.
source: We performed PCA on the shape and appearance feature vectors to reduce dimensionality from 2567 to a concatenation of 340 orthogonal vectors.

claim: The reduced dimensionality feature vectors were used to transform the feature space with Large Margin Nearest Neighbor.
source: This was then used to transform the feature space with Large Margin Nearest Neighbor (LMNN, Weinberger and Saul, 2009).
evidence: Description of transformation method with citation

claim: LMNN is an optimization algorithm that uses a training set of pairs of vector labels and learns a Mahalanobis distance that maximizes the kNN classification over a training set.
source: LMNN is an optimization algorithm that uses a training set of pairs of vector labels (xi; li) and learns a Mahalanobis distance that maximizes the kNN classification over a training set.
evidence: Description of LMNN method with citation

claim: Even if the LMNN system only considers local information, the final metric is global.
source: Note that even if the system only considers local information (i.e., number of intruders for each instance) the final metric is global.

claim: The Mahalanobis distance was computed as dist(xi; xj) = (xi − xj)tLtL(xi − xj) where L is a linear matrix.
source: The Mahalanobis distance was computed as dist(xi; xj) = (xi − xj)tLtL(xi − xj) where L is a linear matrix.

claim: The Mahalanobis distance is equivalent to the Euclidean distance taken in the space after transformation by L.
source: It is equivalent to the Euclidean distance taken in the space after transformation by L.

claim: LMNN linearly transforms dimensions in feature space to maximize the margins separating classes of labeled instances.
source: That is to say, LMNN linearly transforms dimensions in feature space to maximize the margins separating classes of labeled instances.

claim: LMNN should expand dimensions with phenotypically relevant information and compress dimensions uninformative for classification.
source: This should, in principle expand dimensions with phenotypically relevant information and compresses dimensions uninformative for classification.

claim: A series of experiments based on projected 3D faces were performed to validate the characteristics of the transformation of spurious and phenotypic vectors in Clinical Face Phenotype Space.
source: To validate the characteristics of the transformation of spurious and phenotypic vectors in Clinical Face Phenotype Space, we performed a series of experiments based on projected 3D faces.

claim: The 3D facial model proposed by Blanz & Vetter was used for validation experiments.
source: We used the 3D facial model proposed by Blanz & Vetter (Blanz, 2006) http://faces.cs.unibas.ch/bfm/ which allowed us to create faces with a direct control over shape, appearance, lighting, and facial pose.
evidence: Description of validation method with citation

claim: 5 test faces were synthesized at random moving along the first 15 components of both the shape and appearance models.
source: We synthesized 5 test faces at random moving along the first 15 components of both the shape and appearance models.

claim: For each simulated face, a set of 20 images was generated for each combination of 5 head rotations and 4 lighting conditions.
source: For each face, we generated a set of 20 images for each combination of 5 head rotations and 4 lighting conditions.

claim: Simulated images were used to compare similarity measures in the raw feature space and in Clinical Face Phenotype Space.
source: We use these simulated images to compare similarity measures in the raw feature space and in Clinical Face Phenotype Space (Figure 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: A reorientation of the raw feature vectors and Clinical Face Phenotype Space was performed using PCA without dimensionality reduction in order to sort the dimensions by variation magnitude.
source: We performed a reorientation of the raw feature vectors and Clinical Face Phenotype Space using PCA without dimensionality reduction in order to sort the dimensions by variation magnitude.

claim: The reorientation allowed assessment of the relative contributions of phenotypic variation and spurious variations to clustering of faces.
source: This allowed us to assess the relative contributions of phenotypic variation and spurious variations to clustering of faces.

claim: The strongest influences on clustering would be expected to be encoded in the first modes of variation.
source: The strongest influences on clustering would be expected to be encoded in the first modes of variation.

claim: Placing the synthetic faces in the reoriented spaces allowed description of the PCA signatures of phenotypic variations and spurious variation.
source: Placing the synthetic faces in the reoriented spaces allowed us to describe the PCA signatures of phenotypic variations (shape, appearance) and spurious variation (lighting, head pose).

claim: Several dimensionality reduction methods and metrics were used for visualization and estimation of the properties of Clinical Face Phenotype Space.
source: We used several dimensionality reduction methods and metrics for visualization and estimation of the properties of Clinical Face Phenotype Space.

claim: An estimate of search space reduction was developed to determine the improvements in clustering in Clinical Face Phenotype Space controlling for the composition of the database.
source: We developed an estimate of search space reduction to determine the improvements in clustering in Clinical Face Phenotype Space controlling for the composition of the database.
evidence: Description of the CIF metric development

claim: The CIF calculates the degree to which intruders in a nearest neighbor search between instances of the same syndrome are excluded in Clinical Face Phenotype Space.
source: Essentially, this calculates the degree to which intruders in a nearest neighbor search between instances of the same syndrome are excluded in Clinical Face Phenotype Space.

claim: A 20 nearest neighbor linkage map was used to visualize Clinical Face Phenotype Space using force directed graphs implemented through Gephi.
source: We used a 20 nearest neighbor linkage map to visualize Clinical Face Phenotype Space using force directed graphs implemented through Gephi (Bastian et al., 2009).
evidence: Description of visualization method with citation

claim: Protein–protein interaction data were obtained from DAPPLE.
source: Protein–protein interaction data were obtained from DAPPLE (Rossin et al., 2011).
evidence: Description of data source with citation

claim: After conversion to Ensembl gene IDs, 126,586 interactions between 10,442 genes remained.
source: After conversion to Ensembl gene IDs, 126,586 interactions between 10,442 genes remained.
evidence: Reported data from protein-protein interaction analysis

claim: The data were considered as a network of genes, with edges denoting an interaction.
source: We considered the data as a network of genes, with edges denoting an interaction.

claim: The shortest paths between two genes were computed using Dijkstra's algorithm.
source: The shortest paths between two genes were computed using Dijkstra's algorithm (Dijkstra, 1959).
evidence: Description of analysis method with citation

claim: The median pairwise Euclidean distance between syndromes in Clinical Face Phenotype Space was calculated.
source: We calculated the median pairwise Euclidean distance between syndromes in Clinical Face Phenotype Space.

claim: Clinical Face Phenotype Space distance between groups was tested using Kruskal–Wallis tests with Bonferroni multiple testing correction.
source: Clinical Face Phenotype Space distance between groups was tested using Kruskal–Wallis (Kruskal and Wallis, 1952) tests with Bonferroni (Bonferroni, 1935, 1936) multiple testing correction.
evidence: Description of statistical testing with citations

claim: O(r) was calculated from the observations in the Clinical Face Phenotype Space.
source: O(r) was calculated from the observations in the Clinical Face Phenotype Space.

claim: E(r) was computed using probability theory.
source: To compute E(r), we used probability theory as follows.

claim: Under a random ranking for a given positive query, the other Np−1 positive instances are each placed independently among the Nn negative instances, with a uniform discrete probability distribution.
source: Under a random ranking for a given positive query, the other Np−1 positive instances are each placed independently among the Nn negative instances, with a uniform discrete probability distribution.
evidence: Description of probability model for CIF calculation

claim: The expected rank of the nearest positive match is the expected value of Ni+1.
source: For a given positive query, the expected rank of the nearest positive match is the expected value of Ni+1, denoted by E(Ni)+1.

claim: Pipeline code was written in python 2.7 and uses the module Ruffus for task management.
source: Pipeline code was written in python 2.7 and uses the module Ruffus (Goodstadt, 2010) for task management.
evidence: Description of software implementation with citation

claim: The code is available through an open source MIT license at https://github.com/ChristofferNellaker/Clinical_Face_Phenotype_Space_Pipeline.
source: The code is available through an open source MIT license at https://github.com/ChristofferNellaker/Clinical_Face_Phenotype_Space_Pipeline.
